title: Magical Realism
objective: After this level you can explain how magical realism treats the impossible as ordinary, from Gabriel García Márquez's Macondo onward.
summary: Magical realism states the impossible as plain fact. In García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), Remedios rises to heaven while hanging sheets, and nobody is much surprised.

cards.headline: A young woman rises into heaven while hanging out the sheets.
cards.body: It happens in Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude: Remedios the Beauty ascends one day while hanging sheets to dry. In this novel, magic rarely earns surprise. How can a book make the impossible feel ordinary?

cards.headline: Magic, stated plainly
cards.body: Magic realism is the matter-of-fact inclusion of fantastic or mythical elements in otherwise realistic fiction. It's linked above all with Latin American writers: García Márquez, Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar, Isabel Allende. The term began in painting. The German critic Franz Roh coined it in 1925 for realist paintings with fantasy or dreamlike subjects.

cards.headline: Welcome to Macondo
cards.body: One Hundred Years of Solitude (Cien años de soledad), published in Spanish in 1967, follows seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, a fictional Colombian town based on García Márquez's hometown, Aracataca. It rains for four years, eleven months and two days. Yellow butterflies always accompany one young man, Mauricio Babilonia. The world is real, and so is the magic.

cards.headline: Grandmother's straight face
cards.body: García Márquez said his grandmother told fantastic, supernatural stories without ever changing her expression. To write the novel, he found he had to believe the stories himself and tell them the same way. That deadpan tone is the trick. Tell a miracle the way you'd mention the weather, and the reader nods along.

cards.headline: Magical realism: accepted
learned: The impossible, stated as plain fact
Named by Franz Roh for paintings, 1925
The trick: a grandmother's straight face

questions.prompt: Where did the term magic realism first come from?

options.label: A 1967 Colombian novel
options.rationale: The term is older than García Márquez's novel.

options.label: A German critic describing paintings in 1925
A letter from Kafka to his publisher
options.rationale: Kafka's letter was about his cover.

options.label: A Spanish word for Macondo's rain

questions.explanation: Franz Roh coined the term in 1925 for realist paintings with dreamlike subjects; it later came to describe fiction like García Márquez's.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences reads most like magical realism?

options.label: Beyond the seven mountains lay the elf-lords' crystal kingdom.
options.rationale: That's a wholly invented world, not everyday life with magic in it.

options.label: The detective noticed fresh mud on the visitor's left boot.
Grandfather's ghost came to breakfast again, so Mother set another cup.
Rain fell all week, and the river rose up to the old bridge.

questions.explanation: Magical realism drops the impossible into ordinary life and treats it as normal: a ghost at breakfast, told as calmly as setting the table.

questions.prompt: Myths (Level 2) and magical-realist novels both tell the impossible as if it really happened. What sets a myth apart?

options.label: It always ends with a stated moral
It is a traditional story tied to religious belief
It is told as history about one real person or place
It is set in one fictional Colombian town

questions.explanation: A myth is a traditional, symbolic story tied to religious belief. A magical-realist novel is one writer's fiction that borrows that matter-of-fact tone.
